title: A service can resolve DNS but cannot connect to its dependency
description: Diagnose a layered connectivity failure where DNS succeeds but TCP fails, tracing through cloud firewalls, VNet routing, and application configuration.

data.text: The DNS lookup returns an IP address, so name resolution is working. But the TCP handshake never completes. The failure sits somewhere between the resolver and the application port: a firewall rule, a security group, a VNet peering misconfiguration, or a process listening on the wrong interface. DNS success is the first clue that the problem is not in your hosts file—it is in the network path or the target configuration.

data.title: Core concepts
items: DNS resolution only proves name-to-IP mapping, not path availability
TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) must complete before application data flows
Security groups and network ACLs filter traffic at the cloud fabric level, invisible to the application
Azure Private Endpoints and VNet integration add DNS and routing layers that can misdirect traffic
A process bound to 127.0.0.1 accepts only local connections, not remote ones

terms.definition: A three-step process (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) that establishes a connection before application data is exchanged.
A virtual firewall that controls inbound and outbound traffic for cloud resources such as VMs and databases.
A stateless firewall at the subnet level that filters traffic based on rules for IP addresses and ports.
An Azure resource that exposes a service via a private IP address within a VNet, bypassing public network exposure.

items: Security group on the dependency does not allow inbound traffic from the service IP range
Network ACL blocks the ephemeral port range used by the client
The dependency is listening on a different port than the client expects
Azure Private Endpoint DNS is resolving to the public IP instead of the private IP
VNet peering is not configured or is blocking forwarded traffic
SSL/TLS certificate validation fails after TCP connects
From the service host, run Test-NetConnection or nc -zv <dependency-host> <port> to test TCP reachability.
Run traceroute or mtr to identify where packets are being dropped.
Check cloud firewall and security group rules on both sides of the connection.
Verify the dependency process is listening on the expected interface and port (0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1).
Review Azure VNet peering, Private Endpoint DNS, and service endpoint configurations.
Capture a packet trace with tcpdump or Wireshark to see SYN retransmissions or RST responses.

data.title: DNS is not connectivity
data.text: A successful DNS query only confirms name resolution. It does not validate routing, firewall rules, or application availability. Always test the actual TCP or HTTP path after DNS.

cards.title: Immediate Network Test
cards.description: Use telnet, nc, or Test-NetConnection to verify TCP path.
cons: May be blocked by host firewall

cards.title: Packet Capture
cards.description: Record traffic at the client or network boundary to see SYN, RST, or timeout behavior.
pros: Useful for firewall or routing issues
cons: Can be noisy on busy hosts

cards.title: Cloud-native Observability
cards.description: Use Azure Network Watcher or equivalent to test connectivity from the cloud fabric perspective.
cons: May miss local host firewall issues

data.caption: Network path from service to dependency showing failure points
data.definition:
graph LR

    B -->|Resolved IP| C[VNet Router]
    C --> D{NSG Allows?}

    F -->|Block| G[Timeout]

items: Verify App Service outbound IPs are included in the SQL server firewall rules.
Check if Private Endpoint DNS is resolving to the private IP rather than the public IP.
Confirm VNet integration is on the same VNet or a peered VNet as the database.
Review Azure Firewall or Azure Policy rules that may block egress.
Test connectivity using the Kudu console or a sidecar container in the same App Service Plan.

items.question: Could this be a DNS TTL or caching issue?
items.answer: If the IP changed recently, the service may have cached an old address. Flush the DNS cache and retry. However, DNS caching usually does not cause complete connectivity failure.

items.question: How do I distinguish a firewall block from a service not listening?
items.answer: A firewall block typically returns a timeout. A closed port returns connection refused immediately. Use telnet or nc to observe the exact behavior.

data.title: Debug a DNS-resolved but unreachable dependency
data.description: A .NET API running in Azure App Service can resolve sql.azurereview.internal to 10.0.4.12 but cannot open a SqlConnection. Investigate and document the likely cause.
steps: Run a TCP connectivity test from the App Service Kudu console
Check the SQL server firewall rules for the App Service outbound IPs
Verify the connection string uses the correct port and authentication mode
Check VNet peering and Private Endpoint DNS configuration
Document the root cause and the fix
data.expectedOutcome: You should identify whether the failure is a firewall rule, VNet routing, or application configuration issue.

data.title: Summary
points: DNS success does not guarantee TCP or application connectivity
Test the actual network path with TCP-level tools
Check cloud firewalls, security groups, and VNet configuration
Use packet captures or cloud network watchers for hard-to-find issues
Document the exact failure mode to speed up future incidents
data.takeaway: Connectivity debugging requires layered investigation: DNS, routing, firewall, and application. Skipping layers leads to wrong conclusions.
